This paper proposes a fine-grained urban semantic benchmark with dense semantic regions, multi-temporal information, and fast temporal changes, including 2 tasks: semantic segmentation and semantic change detection. In the rebuttal period, no reviewer replied the authors' responses. There are 2 positive scores (8, 6) and 1  negative score (5) finally. 
AC focused on reading the reviews and corresponding responses of 5-point and 6-point reviewers. The 6-point reviewer (Reviewer ozMH) is mainly concerned about whether the code and data are accessible and the 5-point reviewer (Reviewer xrGX) is primarily worried about data available, dataset amount, annotation process, experiment results, and some definitions. In the responses, the authors provided the link to the code and whole data acquisition. Additionally, they also clarified the potential confusion, answered the detailed annotation process, and gave explanations of the experiment results. AC considers that the authors have addressed the reviewers’ concerns well in the rebuttal period and recommends accepting this paper with some revisions based on the concerns proposed by the reviewers.

General Remarks

Dear reviewers,

We would like to express our sincere gratitude for your constructive comments and valuable time. We are encouraged by the positive feedback, which highlights our work as “good paper”, “nice work”, “very well-written and easy to follow”, and “significant contribution”. We truly appreciate these comments. 

Besides, we fully understand reviewers’ concerns about the publicity of the data and code, the issue of transferability, the way of annotation and quality assurance, land use classification system, etc. To address these concerns, we provided detailed responses point by point, from the perspectives of access of code and data, factors affecting the model performance, the value of FUSU data, annotation quality assurance, etc. We also provided additional experiment results (self-supervised learning, loss functions, and other metrics) to provide a broader insight into our data. Some auxiliary visualization data was added to the PDF file for better illustrations.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for your efforts again and we truly hope our responses could address your concerns. We are happy to welcome further discussion and suggestions for improving the paper.

9. As of now the results seem to focus more on FUSU-Net which I believe is not the major contribution of the paper

We show the results with Acc in Table 2 in the attached PDF to offer a broader insight into the FUSU data. we will add more metrics in the Appendix in the revised manuscript. As for the factors affecting such results, we think there are mainly three reasons. First, land use classifications are driven by human activities, so as we can see from Fig. 1, the land use class “Park” actually has buildings, roads, trees, etc., which is a complex and cannot be interpreted from pixel values directly and easily but requires auxiliary data (e.g., population, economy) for a better result. Therefore, the challenges posed by FUSU data are highlighted and the overall performance is worse than other existing datasets (see Section A.5.5). Second, as you just mentioned, the long-tailed characteristic brings difficulties in detecting tail classes. Besides, the tail classes tend to be more difficult than the head classes. For example, the head class “Residential land” may have repeated features within but the tail class “commercial land” has various geographical features. Third, as Reviewer xrGX mentioned, one classification system may not be proper for all kinds of cities. Each city has its own features and a specialized classification system may be more appropriate. The same definition may have different feature representations in two different cities. “Commercial areas” in one region might predominantly consist of small retail stores, whereas in another region, they might be characterized by large shopping malls and business complexes. These semantic differences can lead to discrepancies in model performance when transferring to new areas. This really poses challenges when applied to different geographical areas with varying urban structures and land use patterns. All these factors contribute to the poor results compared with other datasets and make FUSU data a novel, valuable and challenging dataset for the community.

10. Abstract line 13 is grammatically incorrect: "southern and northern region of China"

Thank you for your carefulness. We have corrected it in the revised manuscript.

11. In table 1: it is hard to understand what the third and second last columns (Temporal image and annotation mean). In some cases such as Potsdam and FUSU: it signifies the number of temporal images for each location in the dataset. In some other cases, such as DynamicEarthNet or FLAIR it signifies the frequency. It might be better to have a more consistent column. One suggestion could be to put the number and the frequency in parentheses.

We apologize for the confusion. The temporal (image) refers to the overall observation times of the dataset. If each location has only one observation, the temporal (image) is 1. If observations of one location have X snapshot times, the temporal (image) is X. The temporal (annotation) refers to how many snapshot times of observations are annotated. If two snapshot times of observations are all annotated, the temporal (annotation) is 2. For example, DynamicEarthNet has daily observations on each location, and the annotators manually label the weekly observations. Then we call the temporal (image) is daily, and the temporal (annotation) is weekly. There may be some confusion and we have revised it in the revised manuscript based on your suggestion.

12. In Figure 2, could be useful to add image sizes to the figure

Thank you for your suggestion and we add image sizes in the revised manuscript.

13. In Figure 5a, the dashed blue arrows are in the reverse direction that the usual u-TAEs feed forward direction

We apologize for the mistake. We have corrected it in the revised paper.

We hope the revisions and clarifications addressed the reviewer's questions and again extend our gratitude for the valuable feedback.

Dear reviewer,

We are sincerely grateful to you for your precious time and your feedback. We are encouraged by your positive feedbacks, which is really inspiring. We hope our answers and additional experiments could address your concerns.

1. What does $\mathcal{I}$ in the definition of $\mathcal{F}_s$ in line 164. What does $|$ mean in the function definition?

$\mathcal{I}$ means the input high-resolution image, which includes T1 image $\mathcal{I}_1$ and T2 image $\mathcal{I}_2$. $|$ means $\mathcal{I}_T$ is the prior knowledge, and we use the segmentation model $\mathcal{F}_s$ to segment image $\mathcal{I}$ based on the prior $\mathcal{I}_T$, to get the segmentation map $\hat{\mathcal{Y}}. We re-organize the definition and illustration of these formulas and definitions in the revised manuscript and hope the manuscript is clearer.

2. There are missing closing parentheses in equation 3. I think $\mathcal{F}_s$ is not closed

Thank you for your carefulness. Yes, it is not closed and we correct it in the revised manuscript.

3. The definition of $\mathcal{F}_s$ seems to change, in eq. 1, it takes HR Image and LR time series as arguments, but in eq. 3 it also requires a $\mathcal{Y}$. While $\mathcal{Y}$ is needed for loss calculation it should not be passed as input to the model.

We apologize for the confusion. Our initial thoughts for eq. 3 are that we need to use Y as a supervision to extract temporal information of LR time series. But you are right. This can lead to confusion and discontinuity. We correct it in the revised manuscript.

4. $\mathcal{I}_1$ and $\mathcal{I}_2$ are defined but never used. They can be used in equation 3 and would fix some of the confusion. 

Thank you for your suggestion. We also correct this in the revised manuscript and hope it can fix some confusion.

5. While switching from equation 1 to 3, it needs to be re-defined that $\theta$ is the model parameter used by $\mathcal{F}_s$.

We appreciate your carefulness and cautiousness. We also re-define this in the revised manuscript.

6. The code for benchmarking is not publicly available at the time of the review

Thank you for your interest in our data. Right now the data and the code are available under the URL link. For users’ convenience, we will also upload our data to HuggingFace before the end of the discussion period. But the upload speed to HuggingFace is slow due to the large dataset size. To address these issues, we have prepared sample datasets (including 500 image sets) accessible via the GitHub link for the reviewers to inspect and check.

7.  It would be useful to see the effectiveness of different loss functions

Thank you for your suggestion. We agree with your idea of using different loss functions to improve the long-tail performance. We conduct ablation experiments on this in Table 1 in the attached PDF. We select other two loss functions that try to solve the class imbalance: Focal loss and weighted cross-entropy loss. The results show a little bit better than the vanilla cross-entropy loss, which proves we need class-balanced loss functions to improve long-tailed performance. However, the results of inter-dataset have basically no improvement and we can infer that class-balanced loss functions cannot solve the transferability problems.

8. It would be useful to add more details in the paper about quality assurance, exact working hours, the number of annotators, and the qualifications of all annotators in the team

Thank you for your suggestions. We have two teams for annotation (16 people in total) and all team members have at least bachelor's degree of geography-related fields (e.g., remote sensing, geography, geo-survey). Each team has a leader with a PhD degree majoring in geography and remote sensing. Based on the qualification, prior knowledge and professional training, the annotations are reliable. To ensure the quality, the annotations are cross-double-checked by the other team. The whole annotation costs 3 months and the working hours for each person are about 2-3 hours/day. We include these contents in the revised manuscript.

9. Limited coverage with a relatively small size

We acknowledge the limited coverage of FUSU data. However, FUSU data covers the largest areas (847 km2) and the most annotated pixels (32 billion) compared with other existing datasets, which means the scale or size of FUSU dataset is not small. We can infer that in one city, the geospatial features of geographics are generally homogeneous, which indeed compromises the transferability of the model. Right now we're exploring the possibility of providing more coverage of other cities, and countries. Other regions can have distinct climates compared to Jiaxing and Xi'an and can provide insights into the adaptability of FUSU-Net in varied environments. However, this exploration exceeds the current benchmark objectives set out in our study.

10. Arbitrary land use category definitions

We clarify the definitions of our land use classifications in Table 9, Section A.1. Class “Agriculture construction” refers to land where the surface cultivation layer has been destroyed for the service of agricultural production and rural life, including rural roads and construction land for planting facilities, livestock and poultry facilities, and aquaculture facilities. However the class “public management” refers to land for institutions and facilities of administrative bodies, groups, research, culture, education, sports, health, social welfare, etc., excluding rural and urban community service facilities. For example, an aquaculture pond is an agriculture construction, while a school is a public management area. We have revised Table 9 to add some examples to make the definitions clearer and easier to understand.

11. The classification schema definitions may affect the model transferability to other regions where these definitions might not be easily adopted

Thank you for your insightful comment. We agree that the classification schema definitions can indeed impact the model’s transferability to different geographical regions. Indeed, land use classifications are driven by human activities, so we can see from Fig. 1 in the attached PDF that the same definition may have different feature representations in two different cities. For another example, “commercial areas” in one region might predominantly consist of small retail stores, whereas in another region, they might be characterized by large shopping malls and business complexes. These semantic differences can lead to discrepancies in model performance when transferring to new areas. This poses challenges when applied to different geographical areas with varying urban structures and land use patterns. However, applying a uniform classification system has its advantages. The classification system we use aims to unify national land and urban-rural land management for unified land use management and land use planning in whole regions of China. It means this classification system has scalability, easy for us and the community to annotate other new cities in China.

12. Intra-dataset results highlight a main limitation of the dataset and trained models, which are not able to generalize between different regions

Thank you for your comments and we totally understand your concerns. On the contrary, as for the FUSU dataset, we think the huge differences between inter-dataset results and intra-dataset results highlight the big value of the FUSU data. The heterogeneity of urban landscapes due to urban planning and local climate between two cities makes the data difficult, and this difficulty not only calls for more community efforts to design better solutions for better results, but also has the ability to distinguish better or worse models. [1] also has strong geospatial correlations and intra-feature differences. Try to imagine an easy dataset. All kinds of methods have promising results in this dataset, so no real milestones will be designed and we cannot know which methods are better. As for the model, we acknowledge the limited transferability of our model. However, our initial aim is to release this data and provide a paradigm to construct time-series data. We then offer a new way to fully utilize the time-series data for better segmentation and change detection results. Therefore, the transferability of our model is out of scope. But we think FUSU is a good foundation dataset to help the community explore domain adaptation methods in the RS field (we also discuss this in Section A.5.4), and FUSU-Net can be a good baseline. 

13. Section 2.2 is redundant and check the format of tables 6,7,8.

Thank you for your suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we remove Section 2.2 and add the detailed discussion above into the revised manuscript. As for the tables, we checked the guidelines and found there is no regulations about the formats. We will double-check the guidelines to make sure it is acceptable.

We hope the revisions and clarifications addressed the reviewer's questions and again extend our gratitude for the valuable feedback.

[1] Hong, D., Zhang, B., Li, H., Li, Y., Yao, J., Li, C., ... & Zhu, X. X. (2023). Cross-city matters: A multimodal remote sensing benchmark dataset for cross-city semantic segmentation using high-resolution domain adaptation networks. Remote Sensing of Environment, 299, 113856.

Dear reviewer,

We are sincerely grateful to you for your precious time and your feedback. We are encouraged by your positive feedbacks, which is really inspiring. We hope our answers and additional experiments could address your concerns.

1. Access to data and code

Thank you for your interest in our data. Right now the data and the code are available under the URL link. For users’ convenience, we will also upload our data to HuggingFace before the end of the discussion period. But the upload speed to HuggingFace is slow due to the large dataset size. To address these issues, we have prepared sample datasets (including 500 image sets) accessible via the GitHub link for the reviewers to inspect and check.

2. Explain the accuracy drops in the intra-dataset and discuss the issue of geographical transferability of the model

There is strong geo-spatial discontinuity between the two cities. As shown in Fig. 1 in the attached PDF, the RGB spectral differences are distinct. Fig. 2 shows that even though the locations have the same labels, they can have completely different features because of city culture and climate factors. Fig. 3 shows the inconsistent class distributions. Jiaxing has more cropland and water areas, while Xi’an owns more residential land. Besides, our model does not specifically account for transferability, as our primary goal is to contribute a new dataset to the community and provide a novel paradigm for constructing time-series data. This involves using high temporal resolution and low spatial resolution images to complement low temporal resolution and high spatial resolution images, forming a complete and continuous time series. Additionally, we aim to fully utilize this time series for segmentation and change detection. We hope that the release of our dataset and baseline can assist subsequent research in contextualizing their results.

3. Add at least a third region/city

We appreciate your suggestion and acknowledge the importance of adding a third region. However, FUSU has the most detailed land use annotation categories with a high resolution. It means lots of time consumption and labor work when adding a new region. It is impossible during the revision period, but we will continue this work in the future and we hope the release of this data can inspire the community to work together for better land use annotations.

4. Clarify the definitions of the land use classes and the rationale behind the schema

We mark the definitions of the 17 land use classes in the Appendix (see A.1 in the manuscript). Each land use class has a unique criteria and description, which decide the annotation criteria of our FUSU data. The rationale behind the schema mainly has three rules: 1. Implement unified national land and urban-rural land management, scientifically classify land use types, clarify the definitions of various land use types, and standardize land use surveys, statistical classification standards, and rational planning to ensure proper land use; 2. Maintain the scientific, practical, open, and inheritable nature of land use classification to meet the needs of macro-control, ecological civilization construction, and national land resource management in accordance with the requirements of the national economic and social development plan; 3. Mainly rely on factors such as land use methods, business characteristics, and coverage features to classify land use types based on primary purposes, ensuring that classifications are comprehensive and distinct, reflecting the basic current status of land use.

5. Clarify the acquisition process of the VHR data sources and the level of processing

We appreciate your interest in the data collection and processing. We first have the shapefiles of the two cities, and use the extent of shapefiles to download the high-resolution data in Google Earth. Actually the Google Earth images are all satellite images and already pre-processed (e.g., orthorectification, atmosphere correction, calibration, etc.), allowing us to directly use them. As for Sentinel images, we have some processing steps which are illustrated in Section 3.1 and A.2.

6. Explain how the annotators handled occlusions and shadows during the labeling process

Our annotators received specialized training in identifying and interpreting occluded and shadowed regions. For example, if a road is occluded by trees, the trees will not affect the regular road annotations. If the shadow or occlusion is too dark to recognize, our annotators are trained to use auxiliary data such as reference maps to cross-check and validate the annotations. Besides, land use annotations tend to be more like function zones, and have less influence by shadow or occlusions. 

7. It might be more logical to split the annotators into three teams and use a majority voting system to check for agreement

Thank you for your suggestion. Yes, we agree with the idea of having another team to form a voting system. But there is a practical problem we only have two senior experts to become the team leader. Therefore we only have two teams, each responsible for one city. In most cases, because our annotation teams have geographical knowledge and are fully trained before the task, there is no disagreement. If there are disagreements among team members, leaders will discuss and make the final decision. 

8. Consider hosting the dataset on a cloud platform such as HuggingFace to simplify access and enable online training. It would also be beneficial to add code for a data loader

Yes, we will upload our data to HuggingFace before the end of the discussion period. The code for the dataloader is added to Github.

rebuttal.value:
Dear reviewer,

We are sincerely grateful to you for your precious time and your feedback. We are encouraged by your positive feedbacks, which is really inspiring. We hope our answers and additional experiments can address your concerns.

1. Currently data and code are still not available under the URL link.

Currently, the data and code are available through the provided URL link. For users’ convenience, we will also upload our data to HuggingFace before the end of the discussion period. Additionally, we acknowledge the reviewers’ concerns regarding the necessity of registration for data download right now. But the upload speed to HuggingFace is slow due to the large dataset size. To address these issues, we have prepared sample datasets (including 500 image sets) accessible via this URL link for the reviewers.

2. why do we need monthly data?

From the urban observation aspect, monthly data can provide frequent updates of land use changes which may not be noticeable in annual data. This temporal information is important for classifying land cover types like cropland, wetland and water bodies [1]. Monthly data helps in filling temporal gaps that might be present in bi-temporal datasets, ensuring a more complete and continuous record of changes (See Fig. 1 in the PDF file). From the model training aspect, monthly data provides a larger and more diverse set of training data, leading to more robust and accurate models. Moreover, it enables models to capture the dynamic nature of urban environments more effectively, improving their performance in predicting and understanding land use changes. We show the ablation experiment on whether using the monthly data in Table 1 in the attached PDF file.

3. how does it perform on out of sample city? Is the accuracy drop in all classes or only certain classes?

The comparisons in Table 4 show that while the model performs well on in-sample data, its performance on out-of-sample cities highlights the challenges of generalization in geospatial tasks. This variation is not uniform across all classes, indicating that some classes (e.g., inland water, blank) are more robust to geographical changes than others. It indicates that these classes may have the same geospatial features across two cities. Conversely, other classes like commercial land and industrial land have more variability or are less distinct. 

4. What do we learn from these comparisons (in / out sample)?

The difficulty in generalizing across all classes highlights the need for more diverse training data that can cover all kinds of geospatial features, which is the priority of our future work. Also, by analyzing the performance of each class, we can identify which classes are more robust to geographical changes and which are not. This can guide future efforts in data collection and model improvement. Besides, we think a specialized domain adaptation module [2] or fine-tuning conduction [3] should be designed and added. However, the primary intent of our benchmark dataset is to furnish straightforward baselines that can assist subsequent research in contextualizing their results.

5. how can this benefit downstream urban studies, e.g., POI distribution and density distribution?

The change detection model can significantly benefit downstream urban studies, such as Point of Interest (POI) distribution and density distribution, in several example ways: 1. By using change detection models with high temporal resolution data (e.g., monthly), researchers can continuously monitor urban dynamics. This allows for detecting changes in POI distribution and density over time, providing insights into how urban areas evolve. 2. Researchers can correlate detected changes with the distribution of POIs to understand how new developments influence the placement and density of POIs. 
By integrating change detection with POI and density data, urban planners, businesses, and researchers can better understand how urban areas evolve and make more informed decisions.

We will include these discussions in our revised manuscript to offer a better view of our paper.

6. What is the performance on self-supervised learning (contrastive learning)?

We appreciate your suggestion of using self-supervised learning with fine-tuning. We follow the settings and first train the self-supervised model with 10 m time-series images without annotations, and then fine-tune the model with high-resolution images with labels. However, the results are not promising with a mIoU of 44.15. We think the possible reason is the big resolution gap between the 10 m time-series images and the high-resolution images (0.2-0.5 m) without proper geospatial alignment or correction. For example, [4] is also a self-supervised foundation model with different data sources with different resolutions, but the designed network can unify different resolutions by alignment, and other corresponding modules. Therefore, we think this is a promising idea for future exploration.

[1] Che, X., Zhang, H. K., Li, Z. B., Wang, Y., Sun, Q., Luo, D., & Wang, H. (2024). Linearly interpolating missing values in time series helps little for land cover classification using recurrent or attention networks. ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, 212, 73-95.

[2] Chen, H., Zhang, H., Yang, G., Li, S., & Zhang, L. (2022). A mutual information domain adaptation network for remotely sensed semantic segmentation. IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, 60, 1-16.

[3] Song, B., Yang, H., Wu, Y., Zhang, P., Wang, B., & Han, G. (2024). A multispectral remote sensing crop segmentation method based on Segment Anything Model using Multi-stage Adaptation Fine-tuning. IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing.

[4] Zhang, L., Zhao, Y., Dong, R., Zhang, J., Yuan, S., Cao, S., ... & Fu, H. (2024). A $^{2} $-MAE: A spatial-temporal-spectral unified remote sensing pre-training method based on anchor-aware masked autoencoder. arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.08079.

In general the quality is good, however, I can only give a conditional accept upon the provision of code and data in the rebuttal stage. 

Currently both are still not available under https://github.com/yuanshuai0914/FUSU. 

Also I would suggest the authors to discuss how can be monthly change detection model be used. Some aspects:
- why we need monthly data?
- how does it perform on out of sample city? As we can see from Tab 4, geo-spatial correlations seem to be very strong. Testing with out-of-sample patches does not work well. Is that in all classes or only certain classes? What do we learn from these comparisons?
- how can this benefit downstream urban studies, e.g., POI distribution and density distribution?

title.value: Dataset for Land Use Semantic Segmentation and Change Detection using VHR images and S1/S2 time series

summary_and_contributions.value: I read with interest the manuscript, which presents a dataset of potential significance for both machine learning and remote sensing communities. It includes both Very High Resolution (VHR) bi-temporal images and Sentinel-1 (S1) andSentinel-2 (S2) time series, providing bi-temporal labels that enable both semantic segmentation and change detection. The dataset covers two cities in China, and the authors have presented a solid baseline with corresponding experiments.

review.value: The dataset cannot be downloaded without registration on the project website, compromising the anonymity of the review process. I suggest making it easily accessible for reviewers. I would like to inspect some data to verify the quality of the labels and the co-registration between the data sources, as this is crucial for assessing the quality of the work. Additionally, the baseline code is not available in the repository; please address this during the revision. I am willing to revise my rating if these issues are resolved and the quality of the dataset meets expectations. Please see the sections below for more detailed comments.

strengths.value:
- Includes both VHR bi-temporal images and S1/S2 time series.
- Detailed classification schema with 17 land use classes.
- Usable for both semantic segmentation and change detection.
- Good baseline and ablation experiments.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- Include an honest discussion about the issue of geographical transferability of the model 
- Investigate the accuracy drop in the inter-dataset split to find robust explanations
- Add at least a third regions/city 
- Clarify the definitions of the land use classes and the rationale behind the schema.
- Clarify the acquisition process of the VHR data sources and the level of processing. Are airborne orthorectified images using LiDAR data?
- Explain how the annotators handled occlusions and shadows during the labeling process.
- In Section A.1, clarify how the two annotation teams corrected the labels after cross-checking. It might be more logical to split the annotators into three teams and use a majority voting system to check for agreement.
- Consider hosting the dataset on a cloud platform such as HuggingFace to simplify access and enable online training. It would also be beneficial to add code for a data loader.

limitations.value:
- Limited coverage, focusing only on two Chinese cities, and the dataset is relatively small, compromising the geographical transferability of the trained models as also reported by the experiments 
- Arbitrary land use category definitions. For example, what are the definitions of class 5 “Agriculture construction” or “Public Management”?
- The classification schema definitions may affect the model transferability to other regions where these definitions might not be easily adopted. I suggest adding a discussion about this.

correctness.value: In Table 4, the authors report results from the inter-dataset split with a significant drop in accuracy in terms of mIoU. I am surprised by these results and would like a more detailed discussion about the possible reasons. It is too vague to simply attribute it to differences between the two regions. Moreover, these results highlight a main limitation of the dataset and trained models, which are not able to generalize between different regions. What if we imagine using the trained model on an unseen third region? Could we expect a similar drop in accuracy? This would compromise the potential use of the models.

clarity.value: The paper is easy to read. I think that section 2.2 is redundant and that it could be remove to save space for a more detailed discussion. I also suggest to check the format of tables 6,7,8 is acceptable by the NeurIPS guidelines. It's uncommon to have tables with wrapped text in manuscripts.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The author correctly reported the previous works and limitations of the already available datasets.

documentation.value: The documentation is clear. See my comments above for improve data accessibility and download.

ethics.value: I do not see ethics issues.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value: I do not have additional feedback

title.value: Good paper with significant dataset contribution.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents a land-use segmentation dataset with several key properties such as bi-temporal images and segmentation masks, intermediate low-resolution image time series, and a larger number of land-use categories (17). The dataset is collected using Google Earth (for HR 0.2m images) and Google Earth engine (for LR 10m S1/S2 images). After collecting the images, they are annotated by 2 teams of annotators with dense pixel labels for the 17 categories. A total of around 65k  locations are labeled each containing two HR images at 512x512 pixels and 25 low-resolution images in between. The paper also presents a method to fuse the LR and HR images to perform semantic segmentation and change detection.

review.value:
Pros:

* The paper provided a significantly larger dataset for land use classification with significantly more images.
* It is very well written.

Cons:

* Notations in section 4.1 are very confusing. What does $\mathcal{I}$ in the definition of $\mathcal{F}_s$ in line 164. What does $|$ mean in the function definition?
     - There are missing closing parentheses in equation 3. I think $\mathcal{F}_s$ is not closed. 
     - The definition of $\mathcal{F_s}$ seems to change, in eq. 1, it takes HR Image and LR time series as arguments, but in eq. 3 it also requires a $\mathcal{Y}$. While, $\mathcal{Y}$ is needed for loss calculation it should not be passed as input to the model. 
     - $\mathcal{I}_1$ and $\mathcal{I}_2$ are defined but never used. They can be used in equation 3 and would fix some of the confusions.
     - While switching from equation 1 to 3, it needs to be re-defined that $\theta$ is model parameter used by  $\mathcal{F}_s$.
* The code for benchmarking is not publicly available at the time of the review (at the GitHub link) (Although the dataset is available).

Overall this is a good paper with a significant contribution, therefore my initial recommendation is an accept.

strengths.value:
The paper provided a large and higher-quality dataset for land use classification. Even without the sentinel images or the temporal aspect, the 17-class land use dataset in itself is a useful contribution to the community.

The paper is very well-written, all the figures (including the supplementary) help in the understanding of the paper a lot.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
The dataset is long-tailed, which is a good thing as most real-world datasets are long-tailed. However, such datasets often require class-balanced loss functions for a model to be effective. In fact, this might partially be a reason for why inter-dataset training is doing so much worse than intra. It would be useful to see the effectiveness of different loss functions.

Since collecting annotations is a big (and most expensive) part of creating such annotations. It would be useful to add more details in the paper about quality assurance, exact working hours, the number of annotators, and the qualifications of all annotators in the team. 

Metrics other than IoU could also be presented for these methods (such as per-class pixel-level accuracy) for a more comprehensive evaluation benchmark. Since this is a dataset and benchmark paper, the discussion of the results should talk more about how the dataset is affecting such results. For example, do less popular classes result in poorer results? As of now the results seem to focus more on FUSU-Net which I believe is not the major contribution of the paper.

Section 4.1 needs to be improved upon (see review).

limitations.value: Yes, the authors discuss limitations such as it being restricted to two regions, and the low effectiveness of using SAR imagery.

correctness.value: Yes, the dataset is constructed in a sound way.

clarity.value: The paper is very well written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Prior work including the datasets as well as the prior tasks and models are discussed in detail.

documentation.value: The dataset collection is well documented with sources etc. Except for the human annotation stage (see areas of improvement).

ethics.value: There are no major ethical concerns.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Minor fixes:
    
* Abstract line 13 is grammatically incorrect: "southern and northern **region** of China"
* In table 1: it is hard to understand what the third and second last columns (Temporal image and annotation mean). In some cases such as Potsdam and FUSU: it signifies the **number** of temporal images for each location in the dataset. In some other cases, such as DynamicEarthNet or FLAIR it signifies the **frequency**. It might be better to have a more consistent column. One suggestion could be to put the number and the frequency in parentheses.
*  In Figure 2, could be useful to add image sizes to the figure.
*  In Figure 5a, the dashed blue arrows are in the reverse direction that the usual u-TAEs feed forward direction.

title.value: FUSU: A Multi-temporal-source Land Use Change Segmentation Dataset for Fine-grained Urban Semantic Understanding

abstract.value: Fine urban change segmentation using multi-temporal remote sensing images is essential for understanding human-environment interactions in urban areas. Although there have been advances in high-quality land cover datasets that reveal the physical features of urban landscapes, the lack of fine-grained land use datasets hinders a deeper understanding of how human activities are distributed across landscapes and the impact of these activities on the environment, thus constraining proper technique development. To address this, we introduce FUSU, the first fine-grained land use change segmentation dataset for Fine-grained Urban Semantic Understanding. FUSU features the most detailed land use classification system to date, with 17 classes and 30 billion pixels of annotations. It includes bi-temporal high-resolution satellite images with 0.2-0.5 m ground sample distance and monthly optical and radar satellite time series, covering 847 km^2 across five urban areas in the southern and northern of China with different geographical features. The fine-grained land use pixel-wise annotations and high spatial-temporal resolution data provide a robust foundation for developing proper deep learning models to provide contextual insights on human activities and urbanization. To fully leverage FUSU, we propose a unified time-series architecture for both change detection and segmentation. We benchmark FUSU on various methods for several tasks. Dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/yuanshuai0914/FUSU.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')

reviewer_nomination.description: Please nominate one author who would be willing to review NeurIPS 2024 papers. Receiving these nominations is important for us to ensure that we have enough capable reviewers to review all submissions. Reviewers are expected to have at least two papers in top peer-reviewed conferences or journals, with at least one paper in a machine learning venue (e.g., NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR) in the last three years, though we still ask that you nominate one of the authors even if none meet this requirement. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.
